citation.title: Caffeine improves sustained attention in young adults: a randomized controlled trial

data.claim: Caffeine significantly increased sustained attention scores compared with placebo (mean difference 4.2 points, 95% CI 1.5 to 6.9, p = 0.003).
data.methodology: We randomized n = 120 healthy young adults (ages 18-30, 61 female) to 200 mg caffeine or matched placebo in a double-blind parallel design. Sustained attention was measured with the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) 45 minutes after administration. The prespecified primary outcome was the sustained attention composite score.
limitations: Single dose, single session, young-adult sample only; generalization to older adults is unknown.

citation.title: No significant effect of caffeine on sustained attention in older adults

data.claim: Caffeine did not significantly change sustained attention scores compared with placebo (mean difference 0.6 points, 95% CI -1.1 to 2.3, p = 0.41).
data.methodology: A double-blind crossover design enrolled n = 85 older adults (ages 65-82, 47 female). Sustained attention was measured with the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) 45 minutes after each administration, one week apart.
limitations: Crossover design with a single dose; habitual caffeine intake was self-reported.

Reaction-time lapses decreased in the caffeine group (p = 0.01).
In this randomized placebo-controlled trial we examined whether a 200 mg dose of caffeine improves sustained attention in healthy young adults.
Caffeine significantly increased sustained attention scores relative to placebo.
A moderate caffeine dose produced a reliable improvement in sustained attention among young adults.

claims_b.text: Caffeine did not significantly change sustained attention scores compared with placebo (mean difference 0.6 points, 95% CI -1.1 to 2.3, p = 0.41).
Self-reported alertness increased modestly (p = 0.04) without a corresponding performance change.
Caffeine did not significantly change sustained attention scores relative to placebo.
Routine caffeine supplementation to support attention in older adults is not supported by these data.
In contrast with reports in younger samples, caffeine produced no measurable sustained-attention benefit in older adults.

methods.a: We randomized n = 120 healthy young adults (ages 18-30, 61 female) to 200 mg caffeine or matched placebo in a double-blind parallel design. methods.b: A double-blind crossover design enrolled n = 85 older adults (ages 65-82, 47 female). Sustained attention was measured with the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) 45 minutes after each administration, one week apart.

a: Single dose, single session, young-adult sample only; generalization to older adults is unknown.
b: Crossover design with a single dose; habitual caffeine intake was self-reported.
